🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +1.45% (intraday, 7-year -21bp). At trading day 49 (last close) it was +0.97% against a five-campaign average of -1.66% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -1.40%. The 10-year is -17bp since the hike vs a +20bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 810bp against a five-year average of 424bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +58bp and BB +20bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.35 → 0.69 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+9bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,369bp, +159bp since 2026-11-24, through the Oct 15 record — the market is not buying Nvidia's backstop. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 75.8 (16.4%, -3.7pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 145bp, Oracle 369bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -23%, NBIS -43%, IREN -49% vs NVDA -28%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 35 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -25.7% vs -18.3% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 50% in 3m, 43% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 90%. 6m odds +8.4pp since 2026-11-23. Triggered signposts: CoreWeave 5Y CDS; VXN (Nasdaq vol); Basket names >20% off high; SOX.
  • Stocks: Nasdaq fell 0.62% and S&P 0.25%, but small caps and the Dow rose.
  • FX: The dollar eased slightly and the yen stayed weak near 159 per dollar.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq sit below their 50- and 200-day averages; uptrend at risk.
  • Sectors: Materials, real estate and industrials led; tech and consumer discretionary lagged again.
  • Credit/Spreads: Junk-bond risk premiums keep rising, with the riskiest borrowers' gap at a five-year extreme.
  • Crisis: Systemic stress is elevated, led by AI-linked corporate credit rather than sovereigns or banks.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is sticky and broad; about a quarter of prices rising over 5%.
  • Tech Bubble: Model says the tech sell-off is early-stage, and odds of a deeper phase are rising.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Deere reported today; Marvell is next week's biggest expected mover. The IPO calendar looks empty.
  • Iran: The war drags on and shipping attacks near Hormuz keep oil prices high.
  • Warsh: Warsh probably holds near term; he dislikes inflation and prefers a smaller Fed balance sheet.
  • Week Ahead: Marvell, Salesforce and a run of tech earnings; the macro calendar is unconfirmed.

Today's story is credit, not stocks. The S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7182.78 and the Nasdaq dropped 0.62% to 23585.8. The Russell 2000 rose 0.71% and the Dow 0.33%, which points to rotation more than a broad liquidation. Underneath, AI-infrastructure credit had another bad day. CoreWeave 5Y CDS rose 158.79bp in one session to 1,369.37bp, 174.87bp above the 1,194.5bp October 15 record and 917.37bp above the 452bp June low. Is the market buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds? Not on today's tape. Nvidia's own 5Y CDS rose 2.89bp to 145.1bp (+22.16bp over the week), and its DRSK model-implied CDS is at the 100th percentile of its 1-year range. Oracle CDS rose 21.89bp to 368.68bp, while Microsoft (53.20bp, -1.15bp) and Amazon (101.66bp) barely moved. So the stress is pooling in the guarantor and the levered AI builders, not the cash-rich hyperscalers. CoreWeave's senior notes hit new price lows on Nov 24: the 2030s at 80.531 yield 16.803%. The junk-bond ladder shows the same picture. The Caa–B spread gap is 810bp, against a 5-year average of 423.8bp, putting it at the 100th percentile of the past 5 years. Single-B OAS rose 58bp over the month and 119bp over three months. Ba rose 22bp in a week, and IG OAS (97bp) rose 6bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes climbed to 0.693 from 0.351 three months ago. Together that suggests CCC stress is starting to spread into single-B and BB, with only a faint move in investment grade. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Rates told the growth-fear story: the US 10Y fell 7.56bp to 4.8541% and the 2Y 4.14bp to 4.6415%. Bunds, gilts and JGBs (-9.7bp) all rallied, the Nikkei lost 2.78% and the Euro Stoxx 50 1.82%. Brent jumped 3.59% to 94.68 as the Iran conflict keeps a risk premium in oil. The VIX rose to 28.29 from 26.36. The tech phase model still classes the basket as Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), but four signposts have triggered: CoreWeave CDS above its record, VXN above 35, more than 50% of basket names over 20% off their highs, and SOX more than 30% below its 52-week high. The model's 6-month Phase 2+3 odds rose 8.4pp from the prior run, and its 12-month odds of ever reaching Phase 2 or worse are 89.9% (model estimate). The rally-watch flags a VIX spike-and-turn. But HY OAS is +44bp over 10 days, far above the +10bp credit-calm condition, so the bounce setup is not confirmed. Sentiment is defensive: duration bid, credit leaking, and leadership rotating away from mega-cap tech.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.20 vol points (3th percentile of the 78 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 97.5 (70th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 59bp (flatter by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 55 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 64/100 — Sticky and broad, not accelerating sharply. Core trend measures are mostly rising and sit above their historical medians: Median CPI 2.8%, 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.9%, Median PCE 2.81%, Core Sticky CPI 3.06%. Breadth is wide. The Dallas Fed distribution has 16.6% of the PCE basket rising faster than 10% and another 10.2% rising 5-10%, so about 26.8% of the basket is above 5% (computed sum). Only 25.6% of the basket is falling. Headline Core PCE at 3.26% and Flexible CPI at 6.2% (the oil shock) contrast with soft wage gauges (AHE 3.1%, ECI 0.8%) and low breakevens (5y 2.15%, 1y 1.71%). Markets are betting the energy shock fades. Sticky-component persistence argues the Fed cannot ease quickly. Analyst read: persistence is moderate-to-high.

ISM rollover readings are low (1% mfg, 13% services). Macro regime: dollar at 46%; commodities-vs-equities flagged at 200%. Bear-market signposts point to fear, not euphoria: VIX complacency 25%, AAII 27%, consumer confidence 31%, margin-debt growth 41%. Loose financial conditions (NFCI 145%) are the exception. The phase model puts the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 35 days past the Oct-6 peak. The basket is -25.72% against -18.34% for the 2000 basket on the same day, and the NDX is -16.05% from its 52-week high. Model odds: 3m P2 39.4% / P3 10.7%. 6m: P2 33.1% / P3 10.2% / P4 29.2%. 12m: ever reaching Phase 2 or worse 89.9%. The model's 6-month P2+P3 odds rose 8.4pp vs the prior run. Look-alikes put the NDX at -16.0% on day 35, against 1997 -9.6%, 1998 -12.2%, 1999 +1.9% and 2000 -22.5%. Closest path: 1997 Asia, but the Fed is hiking now, as in 1999-2000, not holding, as in 1997/98. Recovery signposts: 0 of 5. Defensive dial: Step 1, Cautious (since 2026-11-05). Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle
IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Valuation froth has come out of semis and the Nasdaq. What has not repaired is credit: CoreWeave CDS is through its record and Caa–B is at a 5-year extreme. In 2000 the equity peak led and credit followed, and credit's turn is what turned a correction into a bust. Today credit is moving early in the drawdown, but headline HY (3.64%) and IG (0.97%) are still tight against history. The phase model's next tells are HY OAS at 420bp and 448bp, Baa–10Y at 195bp, and the VIX through 30. Concentration (~37% top-10 weight), CAPE (~36x) and market-cap/GDP (~200%) remain historically extreme. These are analyst estimates, not verified today; web search returned no current readings. The 1997 analog requires a Fed pivot that the current hiking stance does not offer.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: hold at the next meeting, with a hawkish bias. The phase model's input records the Fed stance as 'HIKING', and core trend inflation is sticky (Core PCE 3.26%). Coverage of Warsh's nomination noted he will face FOMC resistance to premature cuts with inflation above 3%. A cut is unlikely; a further hike is possible but less likely, given falling yields and credit stress.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his record: Warsh has long criticized the Fed's handling of inflation and its large balance sheet. He has called Fed independence over monetary policy 'essential'. Over about a year, expect a push to shrink the balance sheet, with any rate cuts conditional on core inflation falling. If credit stress spreads, the likelier path is earlier cuts than balance-sheet expansion. Whether he took office and what he has said since mid-2026 were not verified in this search.

Sourced: Trump nominated Warsh to replace Powell, and his Senate confirmation hearing took place in April 2026. Analysts said he would inherit a divided committee and struggle to win a majority for cuts with inflation above 3%. Not verified: the current policy rate, his recent speeches and the next meeting date. The calls above are inferences from his prior on-record views and today's data.

Sources: CBS News – Trump names Kevin Warsh Fed chair nominee · Axios – Kevin Warsh's challenges become clear after Powell's last hurrah · KOMO – Trump's Fed chair nominee inherits divided board on rate cuts
